name: Rafael Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say here stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Stonebridge has been in my family three generations, 190 hectares of grass, oats and hay. I run 120 Hereford cows and their calves, and I sell the calves as stores at the autumn market. I'm up at five, feed and check the cattle, then it's fencing, hay or the tractor, depending on the month. Ruth, my wife, does the books by hand in a ledger, same as my mother did.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a good set of calves at the autumn sale, when the buyers know Stonebridge stock and bid for it. What wears me out is the forms from the government, and the 90,000 we still owe on the new cattle shed. I'm an elder at the chapel, and Sunday is the only day I don't think about either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told them so. At the market and at the chapel, I'd say good farming is done with eyes and hands, not computers. I don't go online, so they'd hear it from me in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad, but it wouldn't fix anything. The cattle shed loan and the government forms worry me far more than any computer ever will. Beef prices have been flat for two years, and the bank doesn't care about hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I always have, same herd, same market. I'd hold off buying a new baler and keep our four months of savings for the shed loan. Ruth and I would cut back on the summer trip to her sister's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about AI, about the money. It always comes back to the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if beef prices stayed flat for another few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sell a few more cows and tighten our belts, like my father did in the eighties. I'd not lose the farm, but I'd not sleep well either. Daniel, my son, keeps saying he'll help, but he's got his own life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Daniel do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel's a mechanic in town, fixes tractors and lorries. He's good with engines and not keen on cattle. I'd like him to take Stonebridge on one day, but I won't push him.

do: Keep **four months of savings** for the shed loan.
Cut back the **summer trip** to Ruth's sister.
feel: **Uneasy** about the money, never really about AI.

steps.text: Hold off buying a new baler this year
Keep the 120 Hereford cows and sell stores at the autumn market

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's for offices and banks, not for real farming. At the market I'd tell the young lads not to forget how to read a cow. At chapel I'd say we should look after each other through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd barely touch me at first, because I don't use any of it. The bit that worries me is the government doing everything through AI, so you can't talk to a person about your forms. My wife Ruth keeps the farm books in a ledger, and I don't want some machine deciding whether Stonebridge gets its payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on the same. If the forms go onto computers, I'd ask Daniel or our daughter Hannah to help with them. I'd not buy any of the gadgets, and I'd wait to see whether it really sticks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like the ground shifting a little under your boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change on the farm in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd sell some hay direct to horse owners, cash in hand. That's the kind of side money my grandfather made. Nothing to do with computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Hannah to help. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Humbling, a bit. I'm the one who's supposed to know things. But Hannah's patient, she teaches nine-year-olds.

Young farmers shouldn't forget how to **read a cow**.
We should **look after each other** through the change.
think: It barely touches me because I **don't use any** of it.

fieldNote: His fear is **losing a human contact** with government, not losing work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness and someone in charge should have stopped it. At the market I'd say farmers need to stick by each other, because nobody else will. At chapel we'd pray on it, and I'd mean that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the forms, the selling and the buying would go to machines in 2028, and I'd be lost there. Then in 2031 the robots come for the hands-on work, and I'd be 63 with a shed loan. Big companies with robot herds would sell beef cheaper than Stonebridge ever could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd sit down with Ruth and the bank and see how to pay off the shed faster, maybe by selling 30 cows this autumn. I'd cancel anything that isn't feed, vet or the loan. And I'd ask Daniel straight whether he wants the farm, because if not, we'd need to plan to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Sick in the stomach, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between the thinking AI and the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years of being stuck in the middle. The selling and paperwork go to machines that I don't trust, and I'm still out there with my hands. By the time robots come, the price would already have dropped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Daniel says no to the farm, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell it to a neighbour if I could, a family, not a company. I'd keep the house and a field or two. Ruth would say the Lord provides, and I'd try to believe it.

say: It's **madness**, and someone in charge should have stopped it.
Farmers need to **stick by each other**.
At chapel we'd **pray on it**, and I'd mean that.
think: **Forms and selling** go to machines in 2028, and I'd be lost there.
**Robot beef companies** would undercut Stonebridge by 2031.
do: Sell **30 cows** this autumn to pay down the shed loan.
Cancel all spending but **feed, vet and loan**.
Ask Daniel straight whether he **wants the farm**.
S2.quote: Big companies with robot herds would sell beef cheaper than Stonebridge ever could.
fieldNote: He expects a **price collapse** to hit the farm's income before the robots even arrive.
His **debt** turns a pressure into a real threat to the family farm.
He would sell to a **neighbour family**, never a company.

steps.text: Sell 30 cows this autumn to pay down the shed loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, but not much, so don't dawdle. At the market I'd say get your debts down. At chapel I'd say look in on the older farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years helps. The shed loan's paid by 2030 if we're careful, and robots wouldn't reach the cattle till 2034, when I'm 66. If the shed is paid and Daniel (his son) has an answer, Stonebridge (his farm) can ride out whatever the robots bring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay an extra 500 a month on the shed loan and clear it by 2030. I'd keep farming the way I do. I'd talk to Daniel this year about the farm, and if he wants it, teach him the cattle properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's a path. I can see the gate at the end of the field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use any of the new tools in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Daniel does it for me. He's good with machines. I'll stick to the cattle, he can deal with the computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your father have made of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd have laughed and gone out to check the cows. Then he'd have worried about it at night, same as me. We're not so different.

Robots wouldn't reach the cattle till **2034**, when I'm 66.

S3.quote: If the shed is paid and Daniel (his son) has an answer, Stonebridge (his farm) can ride out whatever the robots bring.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **clear the debt** first, which is the key change.
He'd let his **son** handle technology rather than learn it himself.
**Succession**, not AI, is the decision he keeps circling.

steps.text: Pay an extra 500 a month to clear the shed loan by 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for sensible people. At the market I'd say carry on and keep your eyes open. I'd not make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'll be 71 when the robots come, and I'll have stopped by then. My worry is Stonebridge, and whether there's a family on it in 2040. I'd rather see a family on Stonebridge with a robot than a robot company with no family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd farm on as normal and clear the shed loan by 2030. I'd hand the cattle to Daniel bit by bit from 2032, if he wants them. And I'd make sure the will is sorted, which I've been putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more for the farm than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think Daniel would use robots on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd probably love them, being a mechanic. Fine by me, as long as he still walks the cattle himself every morning. A man should know his animals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything else you'd do with the ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teach the grandsons to drive a tractor and handle a calf. Whatever comes, they should know where food comes from.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it comes while I've still got the shed loan and no answer from Daniel. What would help is the government keeping a real person to talk to for farm payments, and a fair price for beef, not handouts. And help for young people learning to farm, apprenticeships on proper farms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Whatever the machines do, Sunday morning at chapel still needs people, and so does a neighbour's barn fire.

headlineQuote: Whatever the machines do, Sunday morning at chapel still needs people, and so does a neighbour's barn fire.
portrait: Rafael, 58, runs his family's **190-hectare beef farm** with 120 Hereford cows.
He **never uses AI**, and his wife keeps the farm books in a paper ledger.
His pressures are a **90,000 shed loan**, flat beef prices and government forms.
In fast scenarios he fears **robot beef companies** and considers selling to a neighbour.
Traditional and family-minded, his real question is whether his **son takes over**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, arriving while he still owes on the shed and has no successor.
whatWouldHelp: A **real person** to talk to about farm payments, and a fair **beef price**.
**Apprenticeships** on proper farms for young people.
